q: What is the distributional hypothesis?
short: Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings ('you shall know a word by the company it keeps'); it justifies learning meaning from co-occurrence statistics.
example: Ongchoi inferred as a leafy green.

q: Similarity vs relatedness?
short: Similarity: alike in meaning, often substitutable (coffee/tea). Relatedness: associated via a scene or frame without being alike (coffee/cup, doctor/scalpel).
detail: Window size shifts which one vectors capture.
follow: Which does TF-IDF on documents capture?

q: What are term-document and term-term matrices?
short: Term-document: rows words, columns documents, cells counts (IR). Term-term: rows words, columns context words within a window, cells co-occurrence counts (lexical semantics).

q: Why use cosine instead of the dot product?
short: The dot product grows with vector length, so frequent words look similar to everything; cosine divides by both lengths, measuring only the angle.
follow: When is the dot product fine?

q: Compute tf for counts 1000 and 10, and idf for df = 5 and 100 with N = 100.
short: tf: log₁₀ 1001 ≈ 3.0, log₁₀ 11 ≈ 1.04. idf: log₁₀ 20 = 1.30, log₁₀ 1 = 0.

q: Sparse vs dense word vectors?
short: Sparse: |V|-length count vectors, mostly zeros, interpretable dimensions. Dense: 50–300 learned real values, better generalisation and efficiency, capture similarity and analogies.
follow: Why do dense vectors generalise better?

q: What is the embedding lookup trick?
short: Multiplying a one-hot vector (1 at the word's index) by the V × D embedding matrix just returns that row, so implementations index the row directly instead of multiplying.

q: Give examples of connotation.
short: Same denotation, different feeling: cheap (negative) vs inexpensive (positive); slim vs skinny; 'home' connotes warmth. Affect is described by valence, arousal and dominance.
mistakes: Calling them synonyms in every context.

q: Why is cos(digital, information) high but cos(cherry, information) low?
short: digital and information both concentrate counts on computer/data (directions nearly aligned: 0.996); cherry concentrates on pie (0.019 with information).
follow: Effect of adding 'the' as a context?

q: What does PMI measure and why use PPMI?
short: PMI = log₂ P(w,c)/(P(w)P(c)): how much more w and c co-occur than by chance. Negative values (co-occurring less than chance) are unreliable with sparse data, so PPMI clips them to 0.
detail: Biased toward rare events; smoothing helps.

q: Why do antonyms often have similar vectors?
short: They occur in nearly identical contexts ('hot coffee', 'cold coffee'), so distributional vectors place them close; distinguishing them needs lexical resources or special training signals.

q: How does self-supervision create training data for embeddings?
short: Running text provides labels for free: a word and its actual neighbours are positive pairs; random words are negatives; a classifier learns to tell them apart and its weights become embeddings.

q: Count-based (PPMI + SVD) vs prediction-based embeddings?
short: Count-based factorise a global co-occurrence matrix (LSA); prediction-based learn by predicting contexts (Word2Vec). Both produce dense vectors; with tuning they perform comparably; GloVe combines global counts with a prediction-style objective.
detail: Levy & Goldberg showed SGNS ≈ factorising shifted PMI.

q: What problems arise with representing words as indices?
short: Indices are arbitrary (no notion of similarity), one-hot vectors are orthogonal (dot product 0 between any two words), high-dimensional and sparse, so models can't generalise between related words.

q: How does the context-window size change what vectors capture?
short: Small windows (±1–3) capture syntactic/functional similarity (substitutable words); large windows (±5–10, or whole documents) capture topical relatedness.
example: Hogwarts near Dumbledore (topic) vs Sunnydale (similar fictional schools).

q: Build a simple document similarity search for internal reports.
short: Tokenise and normalise, build tf-idf vectors with log tf and idf, L2-normalise, use cosine similarity with an inverted index; evaluate with labelled query–relevance pairs; consider dense embeddings for synonyms.
mistakes: Using raw counts and dot product.

q: What biases can word embeddings encode, and how do you check?
short: Stereotypes present in training text (gender–occupation, ethnicity–sentiment). Check with association tests (WEAT), analogy probes, and downstream fairness metrics; mitigate with debiasing or careful data.
example: nurse closer to she than he.

q: Why can't a single static vector represent 'bank'?
short: One vector per word type mixes all senses (river bank, money bank) into an average; contextual models (ELMo, BERT) produce a different vector per occurrence based on the sentence.

q: TF-IDF vs dense embeddings for retrieval?
short: TF-IDF/BM25: exact term matching, interpretable, strong for rare keywords and names, no training. Dense: capture synonyms and paraphrase, need training and vector search. Hybrid retrieval often wins (used in RAG, M14).

q: How would you evaluate word embeddings?
short: Intrinsic: word-similarity datasets (correlation with human ratings), analogy tasks. Extrinsic: performance on downstream tasks (classification, NER). Intrinsic scores don't always predict downstream gains.
